<reason>B won by making the motion’s comparison easier to decide: the large fraud and access gains A needs arrive only with near-universal use, and that use is the surveillance spine and breach target rather than a contingent design risk. A’s strongest live route—today’s unrevocable SSN is already worse, and a revocable yes-or-no check can be ubiquitous without being centralized—was serious, but B treated SSN capture as the incentive pattern that repeats at higher speed, not a reason to add a hotter national token. A’s bans-and-auditors answer to de facto mandatoriness and the credit-card analogy never showed a force that splits what convenience fuses.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s Rebuttal 2 takedown of A’s “scale is not concentration” and credit-card analogy: a card authorizes money from one account, while a national credential authorizes who you are everywhere, so cryptographic yeses still map a life and remain a broker-ready signal even under selective disclosure.</best_rebuttal>
